title: The history of octopus colour
tagline: From Aristotle’s stone-coloured octopus to robot skins: 2,400 years of working out how a body becomes a screen.
intro: Aristotle saw octopuses match the stones around them. It took microscopes to find the colour organs, electron microscopes to see their muscles, and a lifetime of brain mapping to trace the nerves that drive them. Today biologists test how octopuses choose disguises, wonder how a colour-blind animal matches colour, and engineers copy the skin.

eras.name: Watching and naming
eras.summary: Ancient observers describe octopus camouflage, and the colour organs get a name.

eras.name: Organs, nerves and mirrors
eras.summary: Microscopes reveal muscles, nerves and mirror plates, and the octopus brain is mapped.

eras.name: Reading the patterns
eras.summary: Field and lab studies sort camouflage into a few types and uncover mimicry.

eras.name: Seeing skin and robot skins
eras.summary: Skin that senses light, the octopus genome, and machines that copy cephalopod skin.

eras.name: Feelings, fisheries and care
eras.summary: Science and law recognise sentience, and India counts its octopus species and catch.

events.title: An octopus that matches the stones
events.text: In his History of Animals, Aristotle wrote that the octopus hunts by changing its colour to look like the stones next to it, and that it does the same when it is alarmed. He also described cuttlefish changing colour.
events.why: It is the first written account of cephalopod camouflage, and it was right.

events.title: The colour carriers get a name
events.text: The Italian naturalist Sangiovanni described the small coloured spots in cephalopod skin that open and close, in an Italian science journal. His name for them, cromoforo, became chromatophore, “colour carrier”.
events.why: It gave the colour organs a name that biologists still use for colour cells in many animals.

events.title: Inside a chromatophore organ
events.text: Using the electron microscope, Cloney and Florey described the fine structure of cephalopod chromatophore organs: an elastic pigment sac, the radial muscles around it, and their nerves.
events.why: It showed that each colour spot is a little organ with muscles, unlike the colour cells of fish and lizards.

events.title: A map of the octopus brain
events.text: After decades of work, much of it at the Naples zoological station, the British biologist J. Z. Young published a 690-page atlas of the nervous system of Octopus vulgaris. A reviewer called it the most complete description of any invertebrate nervous system so far.
events.why: It gave everyone a map of the lobes that see, learn and drive the skin.

events.title: Mirrors in octopus skin
events.text: Studying the giant Pacific octopus, Brocco and Cloney found reflector cells carrying stacks of about 11 protein plates, each about 90 nanometres thick, with even gaps between them. They calculated that such a stack should reflect blue-green light, as seen in the living animal.
events.why: It explained the octopus’s blue-green shimmer as thin-film interference, like a soap bubble.

events.title: A book on cephalopod behaviour
events.text: Hanlon and Messenger wrote Cephalopod Behaviour, which describes how octopus, cuttlefish and squid build body patterns from chromatophores, reflectors, skin texture and posture. A second edition followed later (dates from the publisher’s catalogue; first edition year from memory).
events.why: It became the standard guide to how and why cephalopods change their looks.

events.title: An octopus that impersonates
events.who: Mark Norman, Julian Finn and Tom Tregenza
events.text: Divers filmed a long-armed octopus, new to science, foraging on open sand by day. It impersonated venomous animals: a banded sole, a lionfish and a banded sea snake, and seemed to choose the act to suit the threat.
events.why: It showed an animal switching between several disguises at will: dynamic mimicry.

events.title: The chromatophore, explained
events.text: Messenger’s long review explained cephalopod chromatophores as neuromuscular organs, not controlled by hormones. Radial muscles pull the elastic sac open, and it shrinks back when they relax. In Octopus vulgaris over half a million brain cells drive them.
events.why: It is still the standard account of how the pixels work.

events.title: Three ways to hide
events.text: Hanlon argued that the huge variety of cephalopod camouflage comes down to three pattern types: uniform, mottle and disruptive. A 2009 paper defined them and found that the size, contrast and edges of nearby objects decide which one is used.
events.why: It turned a bewildering skill into rules that can be tested.

events.title: Pigment filters over mirrors
events.text: Measuring squid skin with a spectrometer, Mäthger and Hanlon showed that brown, red and yellow chromatophores filter the light reflected by the iridophores beneath, so three pigments and one kind of mirror cover the whole spectrum.
events.why: It showed how layers of skin combine into so many colours.

events.title: White cells and switchable mirrors
events.who: Lydia Mäthger, Eric Denton, Justin Marshall and Roger Hanlon
events.text: A review of structural colour in cephalopods described white leucophores in octopus and cuttlefish, mostly missing in squid, and squid iridophores that nerves can switch on and off.
events.why: It sorted out which reflecting cells each cephalopod has.

events.title: How the blue rings flash
events.text: The blue rings of the blue-ringed octopus turned out to be inert mirror stacks. Muscles under direct nerve control hide them or pull the skin aside to flash about 60 rings in a warning display.
events.why: It explained one of the sea’s most famous warnings.

events.title: A blue-ringed octopus in Chennai
events.text: A blue-ringed octopus, Hapalochlaena nierstraszi, was recorded for the first time in Indian waters among the catch at Kasimedu fishing harbour in Chennai.
events.why: It means people on Indian coasts need to know not to handle small octopuses.

events.title: Soft robots that change colour
events.who: Stephen Morin, George Whitesides and team
events.text: A Harvard team gave soft rubber robots networks of tiny channels filled with coloured or heated fluids, so they could camouflage or signal, a step toward cephalopod-like skins for machines.
events.why: It was one of the first machines to borrow the cephalopod idea of changeable skin.

events.title: A sheet that matches what it sees
events.who: Cunjiang Yu, John Rogers, Roger Hanlon and team
events.text: Engineers built a flexible sheet of light sensors and colour-changing pixels. Each pixel switched between black and white to match the pattern around it, with no one telling it what to do, in about a second.
events.why: It copied the octopus plan of sensors, control and pixels in one thin skin.

events.title: The octopus genome
events.text: The first octopus genome, from the California two-spot octopus, showed big families of genes for building nervous systems, and hundreds of cephalopod genes switched on in the skin, suckers and brain.
events.why: It opened the genetics of a brain-and-skin system unlike any other.

events.title: Skin that responds to light
events.text: Pieces of octopus skin, cut off from the eyes and brain, opened their chromatophores in light, fastest in blue light, with a peak near 480 nm. The skin held the same light-sensing opsin as the eye.
events.why: It raised the idea that octopus skin helps sense the light it matches.

events.title: Opsins inside the colour organs
events.who: Alexandra Kingston, Thomas Cronin and colleagues
events.text: In squid and cuttlefish, the light-catching proteins of the eye were found in chromatophores themselves, including their muscles.
events.why: It suggested the colour organs may sense light directly.

events.title: Colour from blur?
events.text: A father-and-son team used a computer model to suggest that cephalopods might pull colour information out of blur, because each colour focuses at a different distance and their off-centre pupils make this stronger. It has not been shown in a living animal, and other scientists questioned it.
events.why: It offered one possible answer to the colour-blind paradox.

events.title: The Octobot
events.who: Michael Wehner, Robert Wood, Jennifer Lewis and team
events.text: Harvard engineers built the first robot made entirely of soft materials, shaped like a small octopus and powered by a chemical reaction.
events.why: It showed how far soft, octopus-inspired machines could go.

events.title: Robot skin that grows bumps
events.who: James Pikul, Robert Shepherd, Roger Hanlon and team
events.text: Inspired by papillae, a Cornell team made flat silicone skins with a mesh inside that inflate into programmed 3D shapes such as stones and plants.
events.why: It copied the octopus’s texture trick, not just its colour.

events.title: How papillae hold their shape
events.who: Paloma Gonzalez-Bellido, Trevor Wardill and colleagues
events.text: Work on cuttlefish found the nerves that raise and lower skin papillae, and a mix of muscles that can keep them up for a long time with little effort, perhaps by a catch-like lock.
events.why: It explained how bumpy camouflage can last without tiring the animal.

events.title: Muscles that open sacs in a fraction of a second
events.who: Stephen Senft, Alan Kuzirian and Roger Hanlon
events.text: A close look at squid chromatophores described rosettes of radial muscles that widen or relax each sac in 100 to 300 milliseconds, and found that muscles of neighbouring organs can link up.
events.why: It pinned down how fast the pixels move.

events.title: Evidence that octopuses feel
events.text: A review for the UK government of over 300 studies found strong scientific evidence that cephalopod molluscs and decapod crustaceans are sentient.
events.why: It changed how governments think about octopuses, squid and crabs.

events.title: Cephalopods in animal welfare law
events.text: The Animal Welfare (Sentience) Act 2022 received Royal Assent. It applies to vertebrates, decapod crustaceans and cephalopod molluscs, and set up an Animal Sentience Committee.
events.why: It was one of the first national laws to name octopuses as sentient.

events.title: Counting India’s octopuses by DNA
events.text: Using DNA barcodes, a study of catches on India’s south-west coast identified four Amphioctopus species, two Cistopus species, Octopus vulgaris and Callistoctopus macropus.
events.why: Knowing which species are caught is the first step to managing the fishery.

events.title: Colour change is expensive
events.text: Measuring the oxygen used by octopus skin, a team estimated that running every chromatophore flat out costs nearly as much energy as the whole resting octopus.
events.why: It may explain why octopuses spend so much time hiding in dens and at night.

events.title: India’s cephalopod catch
events.text: CMFRI’s yearly count of marine landings listed about 95,000 tonnes of squid, 97,000 tonnes of cuttlefish and 13,000 tonnes of octopus for 2024 (figures read in search summaries of the report).
events.why: It shows octopus is a small but valued part of India’s seafood.

people.name: Aristotle
people.note: Described octopuses changing colour to match stones.

people.name: Giosuè Sangiovanni
people.note: Named the cephalopod colour organs in 1819.

people.name: J. Z. Young
people.note: Mapped the octopus nervous system in a 690-page atlas.

people.name: John Messenger
people.note: Wrote the standard review of how cephalopod chromatophores work.

people.name: Roger Hanlon
people.note: Showed how cephalopods choose uniform, mottle and disruptive camouflage.

people.name: Lydia Mäthger
people.note: Measured how pigments and reflectors combine, and how blue rings flash.

people.name: Jonathan Birch
people.note: Led the review that found strong evidence of sentience in cephalopods.

facts: An octopus has about 500 million nerve cells, and about two-thirds of them are in its arms.
A chromatophore sac opens or closes in about a tenth to a third of a second.
Octopus eyes have just one kind of light sensor, yet octopuses match their backgrounds closely.
A blue-ringed octopus flashes about 60 blue rings as a warning.
Running every chromatophore at once costs an octopus nearly as much energy as resting.
